doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The singer-songwriter and cabaret scene; working the Vanguard
summary: He did not identify with cabaret and stuck to jazz clubs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: There’s a quote in the biography where you say the way you were playing wasn’t anything that... There were a number of pianists playing in a sort of bluesy, soul piano style, like Wynton Kelly and Hampton Hawes, and you thought you could be understood in that context. But when you started to lead groups after the Bohemia gig, and people started to take notice... There were a number of young singer-songwriters in New York at the time, all very witty, very
capable, very verbal, like Dave Frishberg, Bob Dorough...
I guess Blossom Dearie wasn’t playing piano...
I guess I associate that scene with Greenwich Village, and the kind of cabaret, quasi- theater meets jazz culture there... Is that something you settled into? Did you identify with it in any way?
Well, I used to work at the Vanguard a lot. I worked there several weeks. Colomby put me in there. I worked with a lot of different people there.
You never seemed interested in cabaret type performances. I remember Amy would always tell you should try playing in cabarets, and I remember you just played jazz clubs.
Well, I wasn’t interested in anything that took me out of what I was into. I felt like I could maintain it in...
